strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: the paper identifies temporal ordering in VR sketches as an underexplored signal and provides evidence (Tab. 3: 56.8→48.9 F-score when ordering is removed; point-cloud encoding drops to 30.8) that stroke order materially improves shape generation.

Solid dataset contribution: the first open-access, multi-category sequential VR sketch benchmark (20,838 synthetic + 900 hand-drawn pairs across four categories), with a documented collection protocol (surface snapping, 15 participants, ~225 person-hours) and a learning-free synthetic sketch generation pipeline that scales training data cheaply (~10 hours on a workstation).

Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons against the two publicly available baselines (Luo et al., retrained LAS-Diffusion) on both the existing 3DVRChair benchmark and the new dataset, under both zero-shot and few-shot synthetic-to-real adaptation (Fig. 5), plus a partial-sketch completion analysis (Fig. 7) that reveals an interesting property of human drawing order.

Well-designed ablations covering the encoder design (SketchBERT variant), augmentation strategies, pre-training (which collapses without synthetic data, F=12.0), and alternative sketch formats (point clouds vs. multi-view images), giving reasonable evidence that the sequential formulation—not just the diffusion generator—drives the improvement.

End-to-end single-stage training built on SDFusion avoids the multi-stage alignment of prior work; practical details (generation speed ~6.6s on an RTX 4090, training cost, resolution limits) are reported, and the authors state data and models will be open-sourced.
weaknesses: The surface-snapping protocol fundamentally shapes the benchmark: sketches are projected onto the reference mesh, making sketch-shape alignment nearly exact (CD×1000 of 5.5 vs. 55.6 for 3DVRChair, Tab. 1). This reduces the geometric ambiguity that makes sketch-to-3D hard in practice, and it is unclear how well the conclusions transfer to unconstrained VR sketches drawn free in space without a reference model—a limitation that deserves more discussion than it receives.

The model is technically incremental: a BERT-style encoder with Fourier positional embeddings (adapted from SketchBERT) conditioned into SDFusion. The novelty rests primarily on the dataset, pipeline, and empirical demonstration rather than on methodological innovation; the claimed differences from SketchBERT (Sec. 4.1) are useful but modest.

External validity is limited: all real data come from ShapeNet models drawn by 15 participants with a tutorial and an alignment aid; evaluation uses only CD and F-score on a 400-sample test set with no user study or perceptual quality assessment, and no evaluation on unseen categories or non-ShapeNet shapes.

Some inconsistencies and presentation issues: the abstract/intro claims 'reducing CD by more than 60% and improving the F-score by over 40%,' which holds on their dataset but is misleading as a summary of the 3DVRChair comparison (CD 35.5→25.8, F 26.6→31.1 vs. Luo et al.); the open-source URL is blank ('released open-source on .'); duplicate references ([19]/[20]); a garbled citation ([51] '20121'); and typos (e.g., 'datatset', 'imprecison', 'VRSKTECH2SHAPE').

Whether 'order matters' generalizes is only tested on the chair category in the ablation (stated in Sec. 5.3); per-category results and variance/confidence intervals across runs are not reported, so the robustness of the gains (e.g., 64.3 vs. 42.2 F-score) under stochastic diffusion sampling is hard to gauge.

Comparisons on the authors' own dataset inherently favor their pipeline-trained model; the retrained 2D baseline mitigates this, but Luo et al.'s result on 3DVRChair (trained by the authors rather than official weights) should be interpreted cautiously.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing VR sketch-to-shape methods discard stroke/point ordering, and the authors provide the first open-access multi-category sequential VR sketch dataset (20k synthetic + 900 real pairs across 4 categories), which is a tangible community resource with released data and models.

The ablation study (Tab. 3) is reasonably thorough: it isolates the contribution of stroke ordering (56.8→48.9 F-score when removed), augmentations, synthetic pretraining, encoder design, and sketch format (point cloud and multi-view image baselines), which supports the central 'order matters' claim rather than attributing gains solely to the diffusion generator.

The few-shot/zero-shot synthetic-to-real results (Fig. 5) are a useful practical finding: ~50 real sketches per category suffice for near-optimal adaptation, making the approach viable where real sketch data is scarce.

The cross-modal shape completion experiments (Figs. 6-7) demonstrate a non-obvious emergent capability—near-maximum performance from the first half of the drawing sequence—that is well motivated by sketching behavior and could be valuable for interactive design workflows.

Real data collection is documented transparently (15 participants, surface-snapping interface, ~225 person-hours), and the snapped sketches measurably reduce sketch-to-shape Chamfer distance, addressing the geometric misalignment challenge raised in the introduction.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the model is essentially a modified BERT encoder (with Fourier embeddings) attached to the existing SDFusion generator. Each ingredient is well-known, and the architectural delta over SketchBERT (Sec. 4.1) is incremental. The strongest contribution is the dataset/pipeline, not the method.

The synthetic sketch generation pipeline is purely heuristic (surface sampling, spline fitting, DFS ordering with 10% random skips) and its fidelity to genuine human drawing order is not validated. The paper's core premise is that ordering encodes 'design intent,' yet the synthetic ordering that drives 20k-sample pretraining is a crude approximation (spatial-proximity DFS); no analysis compares synthetic stroke statistics to those of the real 900 sketches.

There are internal inconsistencies and overclaims in the experimental reporting: Sec. 5.2 states the method 'reduc[es] CD by more than 60% and improv[es] the F-score by over 40% on our dataset,' but on 3DVRChair (the only table cited at that point) CD falls from 35.5→25.8 (~27%) and F-score rises 26.6→31.1 (~17%). Also, the full model reports F=64.3 (Tab. 2, fine-tuned) but F=56.8 (Tab. 3, zero-shot); this is explained only implicitly and should be stated explicitly.

A conceptual tension is unexplored: the paper argues that ordering 'matters,' yet the training augmentation randomly swaps 20% of strokes, which should destroy order information. The interplay between the order-sensitivity claim and order-corrupting augmentation (and why this improves results) is never analyzed. Additionally, the augmentation description says masked tokens are replaced with MASK tokens, but 'stroke swapping' is described as swapping rather than masking—an inconsistency in the method specification.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: only four ShapeNet categories, two metrics (CD, F-score) without any perceptual/user study despite the application being human-facing design, and comparison against only two baselines, one of which (Chen et al.) could not be evaluated. Both 3DVRChair and the new dataset are built on ShapeNet, raising questions about generalization beyond this regime.

The 64^3 frozen VQ-VAE latent caps output quality (acknowledged oversmoothness), meaning headline CD/F-score gains may partly reflect the stronger shape prior of SDFusion's latent space rather than sketch understanding per se; the SketchBERT and PointNet++ ablations partially control for this, but a same-generator baseline with a generic point encoder trained to convergence is not fully disentangled from training-schedule differences.

The paper is not careful in places: typos ('datatset', 'VRSKTECH2SHAPE', 'imprecison', reference [51] '20121'), and the open-source release URL is left blank in the abstract, weakening the reproducibility claim at submission time.

Dataset scale on the real side is modest (900 sketches, single sketcher-per-object style, 15 participants), which limits conclusions about user diversity and stroke-style variance that the 'user-dependent sketch styles' motivation implies.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: existing VR sketch-to-shape methods discard stroke ordering; the paper explicitly models both stroke and point order, and the ablations (w/o ordering: 48.9 vs 56.8 F-score) credibly support the core 'order matters' claim rather than leaving it anecdotal.

First open-access, multi-category sequential VR sketch dataset (20,838 synthetic + 900 real pairs across four categories), addressing a genuine data-scarcity bottleneck; Table 1 provides a fair positioning against 3DVRChair, KO3D+, and VRSS.

The heuristic, training-free synthetic sketch pipeline is a practical contribution: it enables large-scale pretraining, and the zero-shot synthetic-to-real result plus the few-shot curve (near-optimal with ~50 real sketches per category) demonstrate real practical value.

Thorough and reasonably fair experimental design: retrained 2D-based LAS-Diffusion baseline on the same synthetic data, PointNet++ point-cloud variant, SketchBERT variant, and multi-view image variant all isolate that the improvement comes from the sequential formulation, not merely the diffusion generator.

Additional capability demonstrated (cross-modal shape completion from partial sketches, Fig. 6/7) strengthens usefulness for interactive design; practical details (inference time ~6.6s, training cost) and open-source commitment support reproducibility.
Clear limitations discussion (frozen 64^3 VQ-VAE bounding fidelity and speed) is honest and accurate.
weaknesses: The surface-snapping mechanism fundamentally simplifies the task: sketches are projected onto the underlying shape, so sketch-to-shape conditioning is nearly geometricly determined. The paper acknowledges that Luo et al. performs better on this dataset 'due to the reduced ambiguity,' which raises the concern that part of the benchmark gain reflects dataset easiness (clean contours on the surface) rather than method superiority; the more transferable setting (3DVRChair) shows smaller but still meaningful gains.

No human perceptual evaluation or user study; assessment relies solely on Chamfer distance and F-score with an ad-hoc threshold (δ=0.02 chosen 'to reflect imprecision of manual sketching'), which may not capture structural/topological fidelity that the qualitative figures claim.

Generalization breadth is narrow: four ShapeNet categories, 15 participants, and shapes tightly coupled to the sketch via snapping; scalability of both the synthetic pipeline (saliency/curvature heuristics tuned per category?) and the model to freeform or organic geometry is untested.

The order-aware encoder is a fairly straightforward adaptation (Fourier features + BERT with stroke/point indices); novelty is more in the system/data than in the technique, and the comparison against SketchBERT is a direct extension rather than a tuned strong baseline.

Minor but noticeable presentation issues: missing repository URL in the abstract, typos ('datatset', 'imprecison', 'VRSKTECH2SHAPE'), duplicate reference entries ([19]/[20]), and a text claim of 'reducing CD by more than 60% and improving F-score by over 40% on our dataset' that appears to actually describe the 3DVRChair results—these should be corrected.

Part of the reported gains likely stems from the SDFusion latent-diffusion generator vs. prior point-cloud pipelines; while the ablations control for the encoder, an ablation with a non-diffusion generator on the same sequential encoding would tighten the attribution.

strengths: The paper makes a genuine three-part contribution: a training-free pipeline for synthesizing sequential VR sketches from meshes, the first open-access multi-category sequential VR sketch dataset (20k synthetic + 900 real pairs across four categories), and an order-aware BERT-style encoder coupled to a diffusion shape generator.

The technical approach is sound and well-motivated: tokenizing sketches as ordered stroke/point sequences with spatial Fourier features, stroke-index and point-index embeddings is a reasonable adaptation of sequence modeling to VR sketches, and conditioning SDFusion end-to-end in a single stage is cleaner than prior multi-stage pipelines.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for a dataset+model paper: comparisons on an external public benchmark (3DVRChair), zero-shot and few-shot synthetic-to-real adaptation, a large-scale user study (38 participants, 1900 ratings) including free-hand sketches, ablations of ordering, augmentations, pretraining, encoder choice, and sketch format, plus supplementary experiments on partial sketches, unsnapped sketches, unseen classes, sketcher expertise, and DDIM speed/quality tradeoffs.

The few-shot results (near-optimal performance with ~50 real sketches per category) and zero-shot generalization provide convincing evidence that the synthetic sketch pipeline is a practical substitute for costly human data collection.
Limitations are candidly discussed, including the frozen 64^3 VQ-VAE bottleneck causing oversmooth reconstructions, and the paper commits to releasing all data and models.
weaknesses: Benchmark construction raises a fairness concern for the headline numbers. Real sketches in VRSKETCH2SHAPE are surface-snapped onto the ground-truth shape, so evaluation Chamfer/F-score is measured against the very surface participants traced. This likely inflates the reported gains on their own dataset (CD 4.0 vs. 13.4 for Luo et al.) relative to 3DVRChair, where the improvement is much smaller (CD 25.8 vs. 35.5; F-score 31.1 vs. 26.6). The paper attributes the smaller 3DVRChair gap implicitly but never analyzes whether the dataset itself is 'easier'.

The central 'order matters' claim is overstated in the main text and partially contradicted by the paper's own supplementary ablations: reversing stroke order barely changes performance (56.2 vs. 56.8 F-score) and scrambling strokes causes only a moderate drop (54.6), while the main-text claim of a 'sharp' drop from removing ordering conflates stroke ordering with within-stroke point ordering. The supplementary correctly reframes this ('consistent sequential structure, rather than a specific human-like ordering'), but the title and abstract do not reflect this nuance.

Only two baselines are quantitatively compared (Luo et al. and a retrained LAS-Diffusion); recent VR-sketch methods cited in related work (VRSS [18], VRsketch2Gaussian [9], Chen et al. [7]) are not evaluated, and Chen et al.'s exclusion is explained but not VRSS. No variance over random seeds is reported for any main result.

The dataset is limited to four ShapeNet categories, and evaluation F-score uses a generous threshold (delta = 0.02) partly to accommodate sketch imprecision, which weakens absolute interpretability of the numbers across methods.

Presentation has notable sloppiness: an incomplete sentence in the introduction ('Existing pipelines to create shapes from VR sketches [9, 41] but treat...'), an empty URL after 'released open-source on', typos ('VRSKTECH2SHAPE', 'Fourrier', 'imprecison', 'datatset'), duplicate references ([20]/[21]), and imprecise wording ('reducing CD by more than 60%... on our dataset' in the 3DVRChair experiment paragraph). These are correctable but reflect a rushed manuscript.

The claim that the model 'remains stable with partial sketches, enabling cross-modal shape completion' is interesting but only evaluated with synthetic prefix-masked inputs in the appendix; no user-facing interactive workflow or quantitative completion comparison on real partial drawings is provided.

strengths: Substantial, reusable contribution: the VRSKETCH2SHAPE dataset (20,838 synthetic + 900 real sequential VR sketches across four categories) is the first open multi-category resource with preserved stroke and point ordering, directly addressing the data scarcity that has limited this subfield (Tab. 1).

The heuristic, training-free synthetic sketch generation pipeline (Fig. 2) is a practical solution for scaling supervision, and its value is empirically supported: zero-shot synthetic-to-real transfer is strong (Tab. 2), and the ablation shows training without synthetic pretraining collapses to trivial solutions (Tab. 4, F-score 12.0).

The core claim 'order matters' is backed by targeted evidence: removing stroke/point ordering embeddings drops F-score from 56.8 to 48.9 (Tab. 4), representing sketches as unordered point clouds or rendered images degrades performance sharply (30.8 / 23.8 F-score), and the supplementary order-perturbation study (Tab. A-1[C]) plus the +6.6 F-score gap on partial-sketch completion give a nuanced, honest picture of where temporal structure helps.

Comprehensive experimental design beyond headline numbers: few-shot adaptation curves (Fig. 5), a 1,900-rating user study including free-hand sketches (Tab. 3), unsnapped-sketch robustness (Fig. A-3), unseen-category generalization (Fig. A-5), sketcher-expertise analysis, and DDIM-step speed/quality tradeoff (Tab. A-2).
Clear reproducibility posture: implementation details, training schedules, dataset splits, and a statement that data and models are released open-source.
weaknesses: The surface-snapping tool substantially reduces the geometric ambiguity that makes VR sketch-to-shape hard in practice (the paper itself lists 'geometric misalignment' as a core challenge). The evidence that Luo et al. also improve markedly on this dataset (13.0 vs. 35.5 CD) suggests the benchmark is easier/less noisy than realistic freehand conditions, so the reported margins may overstate practical gains. The unsnapped evaluation (Fig. A-3) is qualitative only; no quantitative protocol compares models on unsnapped or free-hand test data.

The 'order matters' headline is somewhat stronger than the evidence: Tab. A-1[C] shows reversing stroke order has negligible effect (56.2 vs. 56.8) and scrambling strokes only modestly degrades (54.6); the benefits are concentrated in point ordering and partial-sketch settings. The authors partially walk this back in the supplementary, but the title and abstract do not.

Real-data evaluation breadth is limited: only 400 test sketches across four ShapeNet-derived categories, all collected by the authors with the same interface and tutorial; dataset diversity (15 participants, ShapeNet-anchored references) may limit generalization claims, and unseen-category results (Fig. A-5) show visible prior-collapse (e.g., truck/bed reconstructed as table-like structures).

Baseline coverage is thin: the main comparison is a single VR-sketch method (Luo et al. [42]) plus a retrained 2D-based LAS-Diffusion variant; Chen et al. [7] could not be evaluated due to missing code. Quantitative comparison against VRSS [18] or VRsketch2Gaussian [9] is absent despite being cited as related VR sketch methods.

The generator inherits a frozen 64^3-resolution VQ-VAE, so output quality is capped by an off-the-shelf component; the acknowledged oversmoothness limits the 'high-fidelity' framing, and improvements relative to baselines partly conflate the encoder design with the SDFusion choice (no ablation swapping the diffusion backbone).

Presentation issues reduce polish: the open-source URL in the abstract is missing ('released open-source on .'), Table 1 mixes dataset-comparison rows where KO3D+/VRSS lack CD values and are marked non-open-access, minor typos (e.g., 'imprecison', 'Fourrier', 'The model then predicts' phrasing), and Eq. (4) uses an unusual sinusoidal formulation whose parameters are not fully justified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: 3D shape generation from sequential VR sketches, where existing methods discard stroke/point ordering. The core claim that temporal ordering provides useful signal is supported by targeted evidence (w/o ordering drops F-score from 56.8 to 48.9; scrambling points causes further degradation; order-aware models outperform order-agnostic ones on partial-sketch completion by +6.6 F1).

Substantial and reusable contribution to community resources: an automated, training-free pipeline for generating sequential 3D sketches from arbitrary meshes, plus a multi-category dataset (20,838 synthetic + 900 real sketch-shape pairs across chairs, tables, cabinets, airplanes) with 225 person-hours of collection effort. This meaningfully expands the only prior public benchmark (1,005 single-category chair pairs).

The synthetic sketch generation pipeline is well-designed for its downstream purpose rather than visual realism: SES-based salient point extraction, Bezier spline fitting, culling, and DFS-based stroke ordering with stochasticity. Evidence that models trained purely on these synthetic sketches transfer to real sketches (strong zero-shot performance in Fig. 5) validates the pipeline's utility.

Comprehensive experimental support: comparisons on both the existing 3DVRChair benchmark (with baseline retraining) and the new dataset, a few-shot adaptation study, a 38-participant / 1,900-rating user study covering free-hand sketches, and an extensive ablation covering ordering strategy, augmentations, pre-training, encoder choice (SketchBERT variant), and alternative sketch representations (point clouds, multi-view images).

Honest and thorough supplementary analysis: tests on unsnapped sketches, free-hand inputs, unseen categories and unseen datasets (ModelNet), sketcher expertise, DDIM-step speed/accuracy tradeoff, and candid discussion of failure modes (learned-prior dominance on trucks/beds) and resolution limitations (64³ SDF). The authors also appropriately soften the 'order matters' claim in the supplementary based on perturbation experiments.

The method is sensible and well-motivated: Fourier-featured 3D point embeddings with 1D stroke/point index embeddings fed to a lightweight BERT encoder conditioning SDFusion, trained end-to-end in a single stage. Implementation details (hyperparameters, training schedule, inference timing) are reported at a level that supports reproducibility, and data/models are stated to be open-sourced.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol involves a potential self-advantage: the new dataset's sketches are collected with the authors' surface-snapping tool, which directly optimizes sketch-to-shape Chamfer distance (Tab. 1). Models evaluated on this dataset are implicitly evaluated under an alignment regime the authors designed, and the very large gains on the authors' dataset (e.g., CD 4.0 vs. 13.4 for Luo et al.) may partly reflect the reduced task difficulty rather than the proposed architecture alone. The unsnapped-sketch experiment (Fig. A-3) is only qualitative, so the quantitative generalization gap to noisier 'in the wild' sketches remains unmeasured.

The baseline set is narrow: only Luo et al. [42] and a retrained LAS-Diffusion [83] are compared, and one prior method (Chen et al. [7]) could not be evaluated at all. Given the paper's claims of large improvements, additional independent baselines or a non-learning reference would strengthen the quantitative case.

The novelty of the model component is moderate: the encoder is a BERT adaptation and the generator is off-the-shelf SDFusion with a frozen pretrained VQ-VAE. The main technical novelty lies in tokenization/embedding design and dataset construction; the paper would benefit from more analysis of why this combination outperforms point-cloud conditioning so dramatically (CD 25.8 vs. 4.8 in Tab. 4 suggests other factors beyond ordering may be involved).

Minor inconsistencies and presentation errors that should be fixed: 'VRSKTECH2SHAPE' typo in Sec. 1, 'imprecison' in Sec. 5.1, 'datatset' in Fig. 1, duplicate reference entries [20]/[21] and [4] citation years, a missing release URL in the abstract, and the 'first framework' claim needs the careful qualification that Luo et al. [42] already addresses VR sketch-guided shape generation.

Table 1's cross-dataset 'CD Sk→Sh' comparison (5.5 vs. 55.6) mixes different object categories and collection protocols, making the direct numeric comparison somewhat misleading as presented; a like-for-like comparison would be more informative.

Generative quality is bounded by the frozen 64³ VQ-VAE, as the authors acknowledge; the reconstructions appear oversmooth in places, and this limits applicability to high-detail design workflows that the motivation emphasizes.
